description: Hey Guys! We’re tackling Flame in Freefall and some skills that would be phenomenal to have! AI/ML, multi-agent orchestration, software dev, UI/UX, ecology. Looking for: someone with fire, physics or engineering knowledge, and a storyteller/video editor for our 30-second demo. We are best friends with Claude, love the environment, and imo Interstellar is the G.O.A.T.
summary:
NASA expects a Moon base to run at about 30 percent oxygen or more at 10.2 psi or less. We built an interactive evidence map of the microgravity burn tests in NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) repository that shows what those tests actually cover for that condition, and exactly where the evidence stops.

A user can ask a question such as "Will PMMA burn at 30% oxygen?" or explore a 3D Moon, material cards, an evidence chart, and a ranking of 24 PSI combustion investigations by usefulness for habitat fire safety. Every answer is labeled INSIDE, NEAR or BEYOND the tested range, is produced by code (no language model writes any answer), has every number checked against the data, and lists what is not known. The main finding: at normal cabin pressure no material was tested above 22.2% oxygen, and the closest evidence is three low pressure Saffire V tests at 25.4 to 26.2%.

Reading the verdicts: INSIDE means the question is within conditions NASA tested. NEAR means it is just outside them (within 1.0 oxygen point or 25% of the airflow range). BEYOND means it is outside everything tested, so the data cannot say whether the material would burn, and the answer shows the closest evidence instead.
details:
Full project write-up (view only): https://docs.google.com/document/d/1NonyrpVo_M6VqFkADWXKsrTWFDms_2-OXjP-bLFkCD0/view?usp=sharing

The question

To let astronauts pre-breathe less before moonwalks, the Moon base and pressurized rovers are expected to sit between a spacesuit (100% oxygen at 4.3 psi) and Earth air (about 21% oxygen at 14.7 psi): likely 30% oxygen or more at 10.2 psi or less. That is more than a 40% rise in oxygen over Earth air, which makes materials much more flammable. The burn tests in PSI were flown in microgravity on the International Space Station (ISS) and on Cygnus cargo vehicles, and PSI holds no partial gravity combustion data yet (the LUCI and FM2 experiments are expected to add some). A fire safety engineer therefore needs to know: for the condition we care about, which tests exist, and where does the evidence run out?

Who it is for

Aerospace researchers and engineers, professors, and graduate and undergraduate students who need to see, quickly and with sources, how far the existing burn data reaches.

How to read an answer

Every answer starts with one of three verdicts. They compare the question to the conditions NASA actually tested for that material (its oxygen range and its airflow range).

  • INSIDE. The question falls within what was tested. Real tests exist at or around those conditions, and the answer lists the closest ones with how each ended.
  • NEAR. The question is just outside the tested range: within 1.0 oxygen point, or within 25% of the material's airflow range, of what was tested. The tests are close but do not cover it exactly.
  • BEYOND. The question is outside everything tested for that material, so no test can say what would happen. BEYOND does not mean the material will burn or will not burn. It means the evidence stops before that point, and the answer shows the closest evidence instead of a guess. Example: PMMA at 30% oxygen is BEYOND, because the highest oxygen tested at normal cabin pressure is 22.2%.
  • Fewer than 3 tests. A material with so few tests (wax, for example) cannot define a range, so the answer says it is extrapolated.
  • MORE INFO. The question named a material but no oxygen level, such as "Will it burn?", so the site asks for the oxygen level instead of guessing.
  • RESULT. Questions such as "What is the lowest oxygen tested?" or "What oxygen range was SIBAL tested at?" get a plain fact from the table, not a verdict.
  • Number check. Before an answer is shown, code confirms that every number in it appears in the question, the evidence or the dataset statistics. If one does not, the answer is blocked.

How a test ended (outcome words). Quenched: the flame went out on its own. Blow off: the airflow pushed the flame off the fuel. Burning: the flame kept burning. No ignition: the fuel never lit. Ignited only: the notes say the sample lit but not how it ended. Unknown: the notes do not say, so we do not guess. These are labels read from crew notes, not instrument readings.

Terms. PMMA: a clear plastic used as a standard test fuel. SIBAL: a cotton and fiberglass fabric used in spacecraft fire tests. Microgravity: the near weightlessness inside the International Space Station (ISS). PSI: NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics, the public archive of experiment data. BASS-II and Saffire: NASA burn experiments, BASS-II on the ISS and Saffire in a Cygnus cargo spacecraft after it left the ISS. psi and kPa: units of pressure (Earth air is 14.7 psi, about 101 kPa; the expected Moon base is 10.2 psi or less). cm/s: airflow speed in centimeters per second.

What it does

  • Ask box. Questions about a material, an oxygen level and/or an airflow, for example "Will cotton burn at 26% oxygen?" or "What oxygen range was SIBAL tested at?". Each answer gives a verdict (INSIDE, NEAR or BEYOND the tested range), the closest tests with their outcomes and sources, the nearest outside evidence, a "not known" list, and a gravity note. NEAR means within 1.0 oxygen point, or 25% of the material's airflow range, of the tested range; a material with fewer than 3 tests is treated as extrapolated. Text questions ("Which investigation studies smoke detection?") search the investigation notes and say "no match in our data" when nothing fits.
  • Evidence chart. One row per material on a shared oxygen axis, one tick per test colored by outcome, ending at an empty shaded band for the 30% Moon cabin. The full oxygen versus airflow scatter is available on request.
  • Material cards. PMMA (a clear plastic used as a standard test fuel), SIBAL (a cotton and fiberglass fabric used in spacecraft fire tests), Nomex, silicone, wax, and the low pressure Saffire V tests: test counts, how many outcomes are known, oxygen and airflow ranges.
  • Investigation ranking. 24 PSI combustion investigations scored by a published rubric, with every point shown as a reason. Ten of them have full detail: objective, fuels, conditions, sensors, hardware group, and how each differs from the others.
  • Limits drawer. Every threshold and rule used, in one place.
  • 3D Moon. A navigation aid: each material is a marker you can hover for a preview or select for its detail. It is illustrative, and marker positions are not test locations. All tests ran in orbit, none on the Moon.

How it works

Data. One table of 200 rows, each with a citation: 129 BASS-II tests from PSI-25; 52 flow-step measurements from Link et al. 2018 (kept separate and never used as outcome evidence, because they come from a paper with a different flow calibration); 10 Saffire II rows (PSI-99); 5 Saffire IV and V rows from the ICES 2021 paper; and 2 rows each from Saffire I (PSI-98) and Saffire III (PSI-100). The chart shows the 146 tests that have an oxygen value.

Outcomes. The PSI-25 table has no outcome column. We read outcomes (quenched, blow off, burning, no ignition, ignited only) from the crew notes in the appendix of the BASS-II summary report (NASA/TM-20210011385) and, for SIBAL, from the Zhao et al. 2015 appendix, and every point on the page says where its outcome was read from. If the notes do not say, the outcome stays unknown. If the crew turned the airflow off and the flame then went out, it is recorded as unknown, not quenched. Outcomes are labels read from notes, not instrument measurements.

Answers. Deterministic code: a router, a classifier for the INSIDE, NEAR and BEYOND verdict, and a number checker that rejects any number in an answer that is not in the evidence, the question or the dataset statistics. Text questions use retrieval over the investigation notes with a small open embedding model (all-MiniLM-L6-v2). No language model writes any answer.

Airflow. BASS-II airflow was read from the PSI "Air display" column. Its bracketed numbers and fan readings are potentiometer settings, not cm/s, so we separated them using the BASS-II report. Flows below 2 cm/s are flagged as uncertain, because the report says low flows have high error bars.

Ranking rubric. Solid fuel +3; sub-research area mentions fire, or any Saffire experiment, +3; has a data table +2; flight experiment +2; microgravity +1; 20 or more tests +1. Ties break by test count. This is our judgment, not NASA's, and the page says so.

Checks. 102 logic tests and 14 API tests pass, a validator checks the data table, and we typed 24 questions into the finished page and verified each answer against the sources.

What we found

  • At normal cabin pressure the highest oxygen tested is 22.2% (14 tests tied, PMMA and Nomex). Nothing reaches 30%.
  • The closest evidence is three Saffire V tests flown at low pressure and 20 cm/s: cotton jersey at 26.2% oxygen and 70.7 kPa, PMMA at 25.4% and 71.3 kPa, and PMMA at 25.7% and 72.6 kPa (about 10.3 to 10.5 psi, just above the 10.2 psi expected for the Moon base). We keep these out of the normal ranges and show them by pressure.
  • PMMA is the best covered material: 102 tests, 76 with a recorded outcome, at 13.6 to 22.2% oxygen and 0 to 20 cm/s. SIBAL has 32 tests at 16.4 to 22.1% oxygen and 1 to 53 cm/s. Nomex and silicone have 4 tests each, and wax has 1.
  • So "Will PMMA burn at 30% oxygen?" is answered BEYOND what was tested, with the closest evidence shown instead of a guess.

What it cannot tell you

  • Every test is microgravity. The Moon has about one sixth of Earth's gravity, and no partial gravity combustion data is in PSI yet. Microgravity and normal gravity results might bound the intermediate case, but we make no such claim.
  • The highest oxygen microgravity tests (ACME CFI-G, up to 85% oxygen) burned gaseous fuel in an inside-out flame. We do not treat them as evidence for solid materials.
  • Pressure is recorded for only 8 of the tests; the BASS-II tables give none.
  • The ranking and the NEAR margins are team choices, written out on the page.

What comes next

  • Add LUCI and FM2 data when PSI publishes it. FM2 plans four tests at 8.2 psia with 37, 33, 29 and 25% oxygen.
  • Link each answer to the exact page of its source.
  • Add a side by side comparison of investigations (objective, fuels, conditions, sensors, hardware) and extend the detailed descriptions to all 24.

Tools

Python 3, FastAPI and Uvicorn (API), plain JavaScript and CSS (page), Three.js (3D Moon), sentence-transformers with all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (text search), pytest (tests). Everything is in the public repository.

Use of SI (AI)

We used Claude and Claude Code (Anthropic) to help write code, data extraction scripts, tests and documentation, and to review changes; Muse for part of the answer logic and tests; Cursor for small code edits; and Claude Fable for a first draft of the web page, which was then reworked. The default site contains no SI-generated images or video. The demo slideshow is made of screen recordings of the real site and text the team wrote; it contains no SI-generated images. One optional comparison view, off by default, shows an SI-generated Moon image with a visible on-screen label. Team members checked results against the cited sources, and every SI-assisted file carries a note in its header. A full log is in AI_USE_LOG.md in the repository.
